# Why OT does not win, what in the signal to exploit, and which architecture fits

Scope: Dileo & Sottoriva Task 2 on their `-human` builds: gastrulation-human (29 transitions) and pancreas-human (14). Every check is strict and rolling-origin. Each triple is PCC / P@200 up / P@200 down.

Averaging conventions: `all` is the mean over all transitions, as in the CONTEXT DistBridge numbers. `i>=k` means transitions k..T-1.

Provenance tags:
- **[J]**: re-run or re-derived with independent code by a judge.
- **[A2]**: the same quantity measured independently by two signal analysts; a range is given.
- **[A]**: one analyst's script only, not re-run by a judge.

## 1. Why our OT did not win

On these bins the predictable part of a change is mostly three things:
- (a) finite-cell sampling events, i.e. genes crossing zero;
- (b) the reversal of today's sampling noise;
- (c) a weak one-bin momentum.

Per-gene 1-D OT cannot do (a) or (b), and it dilutes (c).

- **What per-gene OT can express.** For one gene, the mean displacement of any coupling between two 1-D laws equals the difference of their means. So OT can only extend the gene's own mean trend and reshape its spread, i.e. how many cells end up at zero. It uses no other gene and no other cell.
  - [J] I regressed the saved OT increment on quantities any filter already has:
    - l1: the pooled 3-bin mean trend alone gives R² 0.71-0.74.
    - orig: the trend alone gives R² 0.04-0.13. Adding the P(all-zero) shift from the nonzero-fraction trend raises it to 0.68-0.80.
    - The remaining 20-30 % has no value. Its partial correlation with the truth, given the NASS stacker, is ≤ +0.008 on orig and -0.02 on l1.
- **orig (the paper's target) is a zero-crossing counting problem.**
  - 91-95 % of the target's sum of squares sits in the 8-9 % of genes that cross zero [A2]. Observed switch-offs are 86-90 % of what pure sampling, (1-f)^n, predicts [A].
  - Changes undo themselves: lag-1 correlation is -0.47 (gastr) and -0.40 (pancr), and lags 2-5 are about 0 [A2]. Any trend therefore hurts: trend PCC is -0.47 / -0.39 [J].
  - DistBridge wins because of its finite-cell observation head, worth +0.15 / +0.18 PCC [A]. A denoised level plus that head, with no OT and no trend, reproduces it: gastr 0.587-0.588 vs 0.585, pancr 0.478-0.489 vs 0.488 [A2].
  - Pancreas, same masks [J], `all`: DistBridge with OT 0.492/0.304/0.439, without OT 0.495/0.305/0.441. The OT step was chosen in 2 of 14 transitions.
  - The OT push alone, on top of the box-4 level [J]: gastr -0.018 PCC (better in 1 transition), pancr -0.002.
- **l1 (the corrected target) is mostly sampling noise, and its largest predictable piece enters with a minus sign.**
  - Noise budget [J, matching A2]. Shares of noise in bin t / noise in bin t+1 / signal:
    - gastr: 0.37 / 0.42 / 0.21;
    - pancr: 0.20 / 0.24 / 0.57.
  - Noise in bin t can be predicted by denoising today's level. Noise in bin t+1 cannot be predicted by anything.
  - The true change keeps its direction for about one bin: noise-corrected lag-1 is 0.5-0.7 across two estimators, and about 0 beyond [A2]. DistBridge couples over 3 pooled bins, which averages away a persistence that lasts one bin.
  - Pancreas l1:
    - DistBridge without OT: -0.035, paired [J].
    - DistBridge with OT: 0.10 (CONTEXT, unpaired). OT only puts the trend back.
    - The plain last change scores 0.14-0.16, above both.
  - The OT push alone ends at 0.16 (gastr) and -0.12 (pancr) [J]. The noise-aware stack reaches 0.30-0.35.
- **linear** is decided by about 10-30 highly expressed genes and the drift in library size [A2]. There is no transport content to exploit.
- **The richer OT variants fail for the same structural reason.** Both prototypes were reproduced exactly by both judges.
  - Population OT on NMF archetypes: the gene forecast is linear in the change of proportions, so OT minus linear extrapolation of proportions is about 0 (|Δ| ≤ 0.03, not significant). The static SB kernel scores -0.10 against linear extrapolation (p 0.01-0.02). Even the true next composition gives only 0.141 on pancreas l1, below trend at 0.160.
  - Gaussian latent SB reduces to a Kalman predict step with a drift. The factor scores are almost noise-free (noise/signal 5e-4 to 1.4e-3), so the coupling carries nothing.

Things that carry about nothing:
- GRN edges on orig: 0.610 vs 0.611. The true top-200 up list is 88 % / 75 % genes that were at zero, and those have no edges by construction [A].

- Global L and n on orig and l1 [A].

Cross-cutting findings:
- The best gain drifts at almost every transition. Rolling-origin selection agrees with the hindsight best in only 7-35 % of transitions [A]. The gain should therefore come from the known noise rather than from grid tuning.
- Signal variance must be gene-specific, set by expression class [A].
- Pancreas orig: transitions with bins of 50-79 cells hold 39-49 % of DistBridge's score sums [A]. Report every result with and without bins under 100 cells.

## 3. Architecture that fits: NASS (noise-aware stacked state-space)

NASS has three parts:
- A per-gene state with known observation noise R = s²/(n-1). It combines a box pool and an empirical-Bayes local-level Kalman, plus a denoised one-bin momentum term and SNR interactions.
- A finite-cell head for orig: expected clipped target, P(all-zero) and a zero-today flag.
- A recency-weighted ridge stacker, gated by 5 expression classes, refitted at each transition on past transitions only.

- DistBridge with OT on pancreas l1 was never paired: the run was killed after about 55 min. There is no DistBridge number for gastr l1, and gastr orig vs DistBridge is unpaired.

- Design-level selection: the features and grids of NASS were chosen after the analysts had looked at the same 43 transitions. There is no valid held-out raw-count build.
- LatentSB uses the median cell count over all bins, including future ones. Under a causal fix its only significant claim goes from +0.016 (p=0.04) to +0.0002 (p=0.55).
- The judges did not re-run the signal analysts' decompositions, except the l1 noise budget and the OT-increment span.

## 4. Next steps for the HPC run inside their harness

How the harness works: `tack/hpc/dileo_harness.py` runs our forecaster inside their untouched loop (`~/tgl-grn-orig`). Their code draws the 25 % test masks and does the scoring. Output per forecaster and seed is `seed<s>.json` plus `seed<s>.npz` (predictions and test_idx).

The forecaster interface is a `task2_forecasters.REGISTRY` entry:
- `predict(hist, ts, ctx)` returns a vector of shape `(N,)`;
- `hist` holds the raw node features (mean, median, std, frac_nonzero, sum) of snapshots ≤ t;
- a strict forecaster gets `ctx = {}`, i.e. no labels and no edges;
- its `.target` must match `--target`.

Steps:

1. **Port NASS.** It is not in the registry: `nass.py` only writes score tables and saves no predictions.
   - Add a new module `tack/hpc/nass_fc.py` with entries `nass_orig`, `nass_l1`, `nass_linear` and a fixed-gain variant `*_h1`. Hook it into the registry with one try-import line, as `dist_bridge` is.
   - Rebuild every feature and every past target from `hist` only.
   - No GRN and no OT feature.
   - Use numpy RNG only, never torch: their masks are drawn from torch's RNG.
   - Align the i=0/1 fallbacks: in their loop, `hist[0]` is gastr bin 2.
2. **Local gate**, with no torch.
   - Call the ported `predict` on the local node arrays. It must match `design_best-signal/results.json` to within about 0.005 per triple.
   - Re-run the truncation test from `judge1/strict_nass.py`: replace bins > k with garbage; the prediction at k must be identical.
3. **Pre-register** with `pos decide` and a frozen file hash.
   - Primary: l1, NASS full with its 20-config rolling-origin grid. Secondary: h=1 fixed.
   - Orig is reported for comparability. A tie with DistBridge is expected; claim a win only if the paired p is below 0.05.
   - Linear is reported only with its mask sd and the library decomposition.
   - Make no OT claim.
4. **Jobs.** QoS stud allows 1 running and 2 submitted jobs, and no arrays, so chain the jobs with `--dependency=afterany`. Use seeds `1234,42,7,0,1`.
   - a. `TARGET=l1 MODELS=nass_l1,nass_l1_h1,trend_l1,distbridge_strict_l1,distbridge_strict_nosb_l1`. This gives the first paired with/without-OT l1 number. Raise `--time` above 6 h, because DistBridge with OT took over 55 min per dataset locally.
   - b. `TARGET=orig MODELS=nass_orig,obslevel4,distbridge_strict,distbridge_strict_nosb`.
   - c. `TARGET=linear MODELS=nass_linear,trend_linear,distbridge_strict_linear,distbridge_strict_nosb_linear`.
   - d. Their models on the corrected targets (`dileo_corrected.sbatch`, `PROTOCOLS="preqA preqB" TARGETS="l1 linear"`): check the logs first. Finished (model, seed) files are never recomputed, so resubmit only if the job is gone.
   - Also port the recency-weighted per-gene filter as a comparator, because on gastr l1 NASS only ties it.
5. **Score** with `dileo_rescore.py`. Our predictions are scored on their test genes for the same seed, so the comparison is paired gene by gene. Report:
   - `all`, i>=1 and i>=2;
   - tie-aware P@200 (`p_ta`) and its ceiling `p_max`, next to their argsort P@200;
   - `pearson_nan0`;
   - with and without the bins under 100 cells (pancr 3->4..7->8; gastr 2->3 and 28->29..30->31);
   - Wilcoxon over transitions, and mean ± sd over seeds.
6. **Held-out.** Only a fresh raw-count build, binned the same way and never looked at, answers the design-level selection risk. The mouse builds do not qualify. Freeze NASS before building it.
7. **Record**:
   - `pos attempt` entries: FAILED for per-gene OT, population OT and latent SB; CANDIDATE for NASS;
   - `pos checkpoint`;
   - the shared-ledger entry.

**What the target is made of (l1).** It is mostly sampling noise of finite cells:
- **gastrulation-human:** 39 % of the variance is noise of bin t (predictable by denoising, because it enters with a minus sign), 43 % is noise of bin t+1 (unpredictable by anything), and 18 % is signal.
- **pancreas-human:** 21 % / 25 % / 54 %.
- The l1 noise model is calibrated (slope 1.13 gastr, 0.94 pancr). The signal is a persistent trend: noise-corrected lag-1 correlation 0.70 gastr, 0.68 pancr.
- So a strict model can gain from (i) reversing today's noise and (ii) a smoothed trend. Per-gene 1-D OT does neither, and it has no cross-gene structure.

**Where cross-gene structure pays.**
- **Gastrulation** is low-rank and stationary: 53 % of the change signal lies in the top-3 subspace of past bins (63 % at k=8).
  - Strict cross-gene denoising (SVD projection, NMF archetypes, factor-space Kalman) reaches l1 PCC 0.26-0.29, against 0.14-0.18 for the best per-gene model and -0.17 for trend.
  - Paired gain over per-gene is +0.11 to +0.15 PCC, better in 19-21 of 27-28 transitions, p 0.006-0.02.
  - Oracle ceiling is 0.40-0.45. Almost all of the gain comes from denoising bin t, not from extrapolating factors.
- **Pancreas** keeps opening new directions: only 9-10 % of the change signal is in the past subspace (about 71 % in hindsight).
  - Per-gene trend is as good as anything: l1 0.160, linear 0.401. SVD adds +0.013 (n.s.). NMF loses (l1 0.065, linear 0.18). Denoising hurts (-0.08).

**Population OT on archetype proportions.**
- The proportions are forecastable: lag-1 correlation 0.4-0.76, and OT-Markov or linear extrapolation cuts the one-step error by 30-50 % (in-sample basis).
- But at the gene level, OT equals linear extrapolation of proportions: paired PCC -0.025 to +0.029, all n.s. It is not better than keeping proportions fixed in gastrulation (0.259 vs 0.280). Unbalanced OT never helps.
- Even perfect knowledge of the next proportions (K=8, today's residual kept) gives l1 PCC 0.248 gastr and 0.147 pancr, below the pancreas trend.

**Linear target.**
- The top 1 % of genes carry about 80 % of the variance.
- Knowing only the true direction of the library-size change would give PCC 0.44 (gastr) / 0.39 (pancr). That scalar is not strictly predictable (strict 0.09 / 0.13), so linear PCC mostly measures library-size guessing.

**K for the archetypes.** Masked-entry cross-validation gives K=3 for pancreas and about 12 for gastrulation (no low-dimensional mixture there).

**Suggested architecture.** A low-rank latent state-space model across genes (3-8 factors or archetypes), with observation noise per bin scaled by 1/n_cells, a factor-space Kalman/trend, and a per-gene residual trend pathway, chosen per transition by strict rolling origin. Tutti i controlli sono strict: si usano solo i bin fino a t e i modelli si adattano solo sulle transizioni passate.

1) Il grafo GRNBoost2. Sul target del paper (orig) non aggiunge niente: 0.610 contro 0.611 di Pearson in gastrulation, mentre in pancreas il piccolo guadagno viene dal grado dei nodi, non dagli archi. Le accensioni previste restano a AUC 0.886 con o senza grafo. Il motivo è strutturale: il grafo esiste solo per i geni già espressi nel bin, mentre la lista top-200 up è fatta per l'88 % / 75 % di geni che erano a zero. Su l1 c'è un segnale piccolo ma vero. Resiste a un confronto con regolatori casuali dello stesso livello di espressione (0.055 e 0.113 contro circa 0) e vale da +0.01 a +0.04 di Pearson, niente su P@200. Si comporta come moduli di geni che si muovono insieme più che come regolazione con ritardo.

2) Gli artefatti dei bin. Su orig la gara è quasi tutta sui geni che passano da zero a non-zero o viceversa: l'8 % dei geni contiene il 95 % della varianza e il 98 % del nostro Pearson. P@200 non può arrivare a 1 per i pareggi a ±5: il tetto è 0.84-0.90 e in alcune transizioni scende fino a 0.17. Conoscere quante cellule ha il bin successivo vale poco (+0.007 / +0.042, e non è un dato strict). In pancreas le transizioni con 50-79 cellule danno il 39-49 % delle nostre medie e il 54-63 % di quelle dei loro modelli presenti in locale. Il tetto massimo dovuto al rumore è circa 0.88 di Pearson su orig; noi siamo a 0.59.

3) Quali geni contano. Su orig i geni che si accendono o si spengono. Su l1 i geni medi e molto espressi: lì nei geni poveri l'ultima variazione si inverte (è rumore), mentre nei geni ricchi in pancreas continua (+0.32). Un modello che pesa il trend secondo il rumore di ciascun gene guadagna +0.06 di Pearson in modo strict. Su linear contano circa 200 geni molto espressi e la variazione globale della libreria, che non si prevede.

Perché l'OT non vince: il trasporto per gene sposta solo media e dispersione. Così non tocca né gli attraversamenti dello zero (orig) né la scelta fra trend e rumore (l1).

Architettura consigliata: un modello per gene che segue nel tempo il livello vero, tenendo conto di quanto è rumoroso ogni bin (filtro di Kalman con rumore preso dai conteggi), più un modello di campionamento finito per gli zeri. Il GRN al massimo come leggero vincolo di gruppo su l1, non come GNN.

Attenzione: ogni script valuta un insieme di transizioni leggermente diverso (indicato in ogni risultato), quindi i Pearson dei ridge non sono confrontabili direttamente con 0.585 / 0.488.

JUDGE 1: best=NASS (design_best-signal) is the best design: 6.5/10, against PopOT 4.2 and LatentSB 2.6. Scoring axes: A, beats trend and DistBridge where it matters (l1 on both datasets, orig for comparability), 5 pts; B, genuinely uses OT/SB and it contributes, 2 pts; C, interpretable, 1.5; D, feasible, strict and reproducible, 1.5.

NASS is the only design that is strict (bit-exact truncation test), reproduces (|d| <= 0.0022), survives an independent re-implementation with other masks, and beats plain trend on the corrected primary target in both datasets. l1 i>=2: gastr 0.335 vs -0.179 and pancreas 0.308 vs 0.135; my code gives 0.324 / 0.297. It also beats CONTEXT DistBridge on pancreas l1 (0.29 vs 0.10, unpaired) and the paired level+obs reproduction of DistBridge on orig (+0.024 / +0.051).

It scores 0 on OT/SB because it uses none. It loses pancreas linear (-0.126, p=0.007). On gastr l1 it only matches the per-gene regime filter. Its design choices were made after looking at the same 43 transitions.

PopOT ranks above LatentSB for four reasons: it genuinely uses OT, UOT and SB; it is strict; it reproduces exactly; and it reports honestly. LatentSB uses future cell counts (nmed), and its one positive result vanishes under the strict fix.

Averaging conventions: i>=2 for NASS and my re-implementation, i>=1 for LatentSB and PopOT, 'all' for CONTEXT DistBridge. No design was compared with DistBridge on paired masks.

The other files are diff_results.py/.json, strict_nass.py, strict_lsb.py, strict_popot.py (and their .json), indep\indep.py with indep\indep_results.json, ot_span.py/.json, ot_standalone.py/.json, noise_share.py/.json, the rerun_* folders and heldout_nass\. No existing file was edited.
WHY OT DID NOT WIN: On the '-human' builds the change from bin t to bin t+1 is mostly finite-cell sampling noise. Per-gene 1-D OT can only extrapolate a gene's own mean trend and reshape its spread, so it targets the wrong thing.

1. **The noise budget, checked independently.** I used the delta method with Var(mean) = s^2/(n-1). Share of the l1 variance carried by noise of bin t, noise of bin t+1, and the rest:
   - gastr: 0.37 / 0.42, leaving 0.21 for signal;
   - pancreas: 0.20 / 0.24, leaving 0.57.

   Bin-t noise enters the change with a minus sign, so the predictable part is mainly reversal of today's noise, plus a short one-bin momentum. On orig, 91-94 % of the variance is zero-crossings, which are set by (1-f)^n.

   So trend extrapolation is wrong or weak:
   - lag-1 correlation of observed changes: l1 -0.17 / +0.16, orig -0.47 / -0.40;
   - trend PCC: orig -0.47 / -0.39, l1 -0.18 / +0.14.

2. **Per-gene OT is mostly that trend.** I regressed the saved OT/SB increment on quantities any filter already has:
   - l1: the pooled 3-bin mean trend alone gives R^2 0.71-0.74;
   - orig: the trend alone gives R^2 0.04-0.13; adding the P(all-zero) shift from the nonzero-fraction trend raises it to 0.68-0.80.

   The remaining 20-30 % (spread reshaping and target nonlinearity) has no value. Its partial correlation with the truth, given the stacker, is <= +0.008 on orig and -0.02 on l1.

   On its own, on top of the box-4 level, the OT push:
   - hurts orig: gastr -0.018 (better in 1 of 27 transitions), pancreas -0.002;
   - raises l1 only to 0.16 (gastr) and -0.12 (pancreas). That is below trend on pancreas (0.14) and about half the noise-aware stack (0.32-0.35 / 0.30).

3. **Population OT and latent SB fail for the same structural reason.**
   - Genes see composition only through the change in proportions: OT minus linear extrapolation of proportions is about 0 (n.s.), and even oracle proportions give only 0.141 on pancreas l1.
   - Gaussian latent SB reduces to a Kalman drift: the factor scores are almost noise-free and the coupling adds nothing.

4. **What exploits the signal.** Three things together:
   - denoising today's level with the known noise s^2/n;
   - a finite-cell observation head for zero-crossings;
   - a recency-weighted, expression-level-gated mix of reversion and one-bin momentum.

   My independent code confirms this: l1 0.32-0.35 (gastr) and 0.30 (pancreas) vs trend -0.18 / 0.14.

   On the non-human builds, which are library-normalised and have no count noise (s^2/m about 0.03), trend is strong (l1 0.52-0.57) and NASS only ties it. This is consistent with the advantage on the benchmark coming from modelling finite-cell sampling, not from any transport structure.

**Implied architecture:** a known-noise per-gene state-space model, a finite-cell head, and an adaptive gain. OT/SB should be revisited only with cell-level data, scored as an increment over that baseline.

JUDGE 2: best=NASS (design_best-signal). It is the only design that beats both the trend and our DistBridge on the corrected l1 target in both datasets. The comparison is paired, reproduced to within 0.0025, re-implemented with independent code and robust to the mask seed. Limits: on orig it ties DistBridge (paired +0.014, p=0.63); it loses to trend on pancreas linear (p=0.007); on gastr it only ties the variance analyst's regime filter; there is no valid held-out test; and it does not use OT/SB.
WHY OT DID NOT WIN: Short answer: per-gene OT can do only two things, and the predictable signal in these bins lies in neither of them.

1) What per-gene OT can do. For one gene, the mean displacement of ANY coupling between two 1-D laws equals the difference of their means. So per-gene OT can only (a) extend the gene's mean trend and (b) reshape its spread, i.e. how many cells end up at zero. It uses no other gene and no other cell.

2) The paper's target (orig). 91-94 % of the variance comes from the 8-9 % of genes that switch between zero and nonzero. Whether a gene crosses is set by the chance that all n cells of the next bin are zero, (1-f)^n. That is a counting fact, and DistBridge's finite-cell observation head already carries it (worth +0.15/+0.18 PCC). Changes also undo themselves at the next step: lag-1 correlation -0.47 gastr, -0.40 pancr, nothing at lags 2-5. So any trend makes it worse. Measured here on the same masks: DistBridge pancreas orig scores 0.492 with OT and 0.495 without, and the OT step was selected in only 2 of 14 transitions.

3) The corrected target (l1). Most of a change is noise from sampling finite cells: 80 % in gastr, 46 % in pancr. Today's bin noise enters the change with a minus sign, so the biggest predictable piece is cancelling today's noise, not moving mass. The true change keeps its direction for only one bin (lag-1 about +0.5 to +0.6, about 0 after that). DistBridge couples over 3 pooled bins and dilutes this. That is why, on pancreas l1, DistBridge with OT (0.10, CONTEXT) beats DistBridge without OT (-0.035, my paired run), because OT brings the trend back, yet still loses to the plain last change (0.14). A per-gene filter does much better: noise known from the counts (s^2/n), a gain that depends on expression level, refitted on recent transitions. It reaches 0.31 on pancreas and 0.32 on gastr, against trend 0.14 and -0.18 (my independent re-implementation, p=0.003 and p<1e-4). Adding the OT increment as an extra feature adds nothing (partial correlation +0.008 / -0.020).

4) Noise control check. When the noise drops, the picture shifts toward trend. Merging gastr bins in pairs lifts trend on l1 from -0.18 to 0.20/0.25, and the filter's lead shrinks to +0.05/+0.14 (not significant). On Dileo's mouse builds, which hold smoothed values rather than counts, trend reaches 0.50-0.53 and nothing beats it. That is only consistent with the picture, not proof, because the smoothing may blend neighbouring bins. So a model that extrapolates, which is what per-gene OT is, would make sense on already denoised data, not on these raw bins.

5) The linear target. About 10-30 highly expressed genes and the library-size drift decide it. There is no transport to exploit, and the trend wins on pancreas.

6) The richer OT variants also fail, by construction.
- Population OT on archetypes: the gene forecast is linear in the change of composition, so OT minus linear extrapolation is about 0 (at most 0.03, n.s.). Even the true composition of the next bin stays below the trend on pancreas l1 (0.141 vs 0.160).
- Gaussian latent SB: it equals a Kalman predict step, so only the drift matters. The factor model loses to the per-gene filter on pancreas (-0.10).

What to latch onto, and the architecture that fits:
- (i) a finite-cell observation head, P(zero) from n and f, for orig;
- (ii) a per-gene state whose noise is taken from the counts (s^2/n), which cancels today's noise;
- (iii) an expression-level-dependent gain refitted on the last transitions, which decides how much one-bin momentum to keep;
- (iv) at most a light gene-module or GRN term on l1 (+0.02, not yet significant).

That is the NASS scheme. OT/SB would make sense only with single-cell data, where coupling cells across bins could see branch and composition shifts (pancreas). It should be scored as an increment over NASS.
